payload.request:
Build a URL shortener service.

POST /api/v1/links accepts JSON with `url` (required), `alias` (optional) and `expiresAt`
(optional, ISO-8601 UTC). It returns 201 with the short code and the absolute short URL. A
requested alias that is already taken returns 409 and creates nothing.

GET /{code} returns 302 Found to the original URL and increments that link's click count. An
unknown code returns 404. A link past its expiry returns 410 Gone.

GET /api/v1/links/{code}/stats returns the code, the original URL, the creation time, the
expiry if one is set, and the click count.

Reject with 400 any URL whose scheme is not http or https. Reject with 400 any URL whose host
is an IP literal in a loopback, link-local, or RFC 1918 private range. Do not perform DNS
resolution; check the literal host only.

Persist links in SQLite. Generate codes as base62 over a monotonic identifier.

payload.question: Whether to block IPv6 loopback/link-local/unique-local addresses alongside the explicitly named IPv4 loopback/link-local/RFC1918 ranges

options.name: IPv4-only literal reading
options.summary: Only check the IPv4 ranges named in the request; any IPv6 literal (including ::1) passes validation.
options.rejectedBecause: Leaves an SSRF hole for IPv6 loopback/link-local/ULA addresses that is functionally identical to the IPv4 case the request is clearly trying to close; a silent gap here is a security defect, not a style choice.

options.name: Extend to IPv6 analogues
options.summary: Block ::1 (loopback), fe80::/10 (link-local), and fc00::/7 (unique local) in addition to the named IPv4 ranges.

payload.rationale: The request's intent is clearly SSRF/local-target prevention; RFC 1918 is an IPv4-specific term but the underlying goal applies equally to IPv6, and extending coverage is the conventional secure default.

payload.question: How the service determines the host/scheme used to build the 'absolute short URL' returned by POST /api/v1/links

options.name: Configured base URL
options.summary: Read a fixed base URL (scheme+host+port) from service configuration/environment and prepend it to the code.

options.name: Derived from request headers
options.summary: Build the absolute URL from the incoming request's Host or X-Forwarded-Host header.
options.rejectedBecause: Trusting client-supplied Host headers to construct a URL that will be persisted/returned invites host-header-injection style abuse and produces non-deterministic output depending on how the service is fronted.

payload.rationale: A fixed, operator-controlled base URL is deterministic, safe by default, and the conventional approach for services that must mint absolute URLs.

payload.question: What character set a user-supplied custom alias may use

options.name: Base62 charset (same as generated codes)
options.summary: Restrict aliases to [A-Za-z0-9], the same alphabet used for generated codes.

options.name: Broad URL-safe charset
options.summary: Allow any URL-path-safe string (e.g. hyphens, underscores, unicode) as an alias.
options.rejectedBecause: Widens the code space beyond what the generator ever produces, complicates routing/escaping, and doesn't change the product's behavior in any way the requester is likely to care about — but a choice still has to be made and recorded.

payload.rationale: Keeps aliases and generated codes in one uniform, unambiguous key space stored in the same column with a single uniqueness constraint, simplifying collision handling.

payload.question: How do we guarantee that alias/generated-code uniqueness (AC4, AC19) and click-count increments (AC12, AC15) are correct under concurrent requests, given SQLite's single-writer model?

options.name: Native SQLite serialization + unique constraint + bounded retry
options.summary: Rely on SQLite's own write locking (WAL mode, busy_timeout, IMMEDIATE transactions) and a UNIQUE constraint on a single shared `code` column; catch constraint violations as the 409 signal; for generated codes, retry with a fresh autoincrement id on the rare collision with a pre-existing alias.

options.name: Application-level global write mutex
options.summary: Serialize all writes in-process with a SemaphoreSlim before touching SQLite at all.
options.rejectedBecause: Duplicates a guarantee SQLite already gives via unique index + IMMEDIATE transactions; still needs the same alias/generated-code collision handling on top, so it adds a whole lock-management layer without removing any complexity, and widens the locked section to the whole request handler rather than just the DB write.

options.name: Separate counter table for monotonic IDs
options.summary: Maintain an explicit counter row, incremented in its own transaction, decoupled from the links table's own primary key.
options.rejectedBecause: Adds a second write and a second lock acquisition per request for no benefit: SQLite's AUTOINCREMENT rowid is already a durable, gap-tolerant monotonic sequence, and splitting it out only creates a second place the two writes could get out of sync.

options.name: Optimistic pre-check (SELECT then INSERT)
options.summary: Check whether an alias exists with a SELECT, then INSERT if it doesn't.
options.rejectedBecause: Classic TOCTOU race — two concurrent requests for the same alias can both pass the SELECT before either INSERTs, directly failing AC19.

options.name: Design for multi-instance / distributed coordination
options.summary: Add distributed locking or move to a client/server database so multiple app instances could share write load.
options.rejectedBecause: Explicitly out of scope — the requirements name a single SQLite instance, and SQLite's file locking doesn't extend across processes or machines anyway, so this would be unused complexity for a requirement nobody asked for.

payload.chosen: Native SQLite serialization + unique constraint + bounded retry
payload.rationale: It gives the exact correctness AC19 demands (a DB-level constraint that cannot be raced) with the least code, matches the single-instance scope stated in the NFRs precisely, and needs no additional locking primitives — at the cost of write throughput being bounded by SQLite's single-writer model and a small, well-understood retry surface for the alias/generated-code collision case.
